title: CN-lab-03.1: Connect Network NS to Root
markdown:
# CN-lab-03.1: Connect Network NS to Root (Part 1 — Default Gateway Setup)

So far you have learned to create a network namespace, give it a veth pair, and reach it from the host over a single directly-connected subnet. That is enough to talk to *one* neighbour — the host's end of the veth cable. But a real workload inside a namespace almost never needs to talk only to its immediate neighbour. It needs to reach addresses nobody told it about in advance: a database on another subnet, a service three hops away, the public internet. For that, the namespace needs a **default route** — a standing instruction that says "if nothing more specific matches, send it here."

This is the first of a two-part lab. Here, you build the default route. In Part 2, you will learn to verify it, break it on purpose, and fix it — the way you would troubleshoot a real routing problem in production.

By the end of this lab, you will be able to:

- Rebuild the namespace + veth pair pattern from memory, quickly
- Explain why a namespace's routing table starts with only one entry (the directly-connected subnet) and nothing else
- Add a default route inside a namespace, pointing at the host side of the veth pair
- Use `ip route get` to prove, without sending a single packet, that traffic to an arbitrary outside address now has a path

## The Scenario: app-ns Needs a Way Out

You are setting up `app-ns`, a namespace representing a small application server. It needs to reach two kinds of destinations:

1. **10.30.0.1** — the host side of its own veth pair. Directly connected, no gateway needed.
2. **Everything else** — any other address, including ones that don't exist yet in this lab's simulated world. For these, `app-ns` needs to hand the packet to something that knows what to do with it — its **gateway**.

| What | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `veth-app` | Namespace-side interface — app-ns's own NIC |
| `veth-root` | Host-side interface — acts as app-ns's gateway into the root namespace |
| `10.30.0.2/24` | Address assigned to `veth-app` — app-ns's own address |
| `10.30.0.1/24` | Address assigned to `veth-root` — app-ns's gateway address |
| `app-ns` | The network namespace being configured |

"Root" here means the **root network namespace** — the host's own, default network namespace, the one your SSH session lives in. Every other namespace is, by comparison, a child sandbox. Connecting a namespace "to root" means giving it a path through the host's own namespace, so it can eventually reach anything the host itself can reach.

## Part 1: Rebuilding the Namespace (Quick Recap)

You have done this before. Move quickly — the new material starts in Part 2.

```bash
sudo ip netns add app-ns
sudo ip link add veth-root type veth peer name veth-app
sudo ip link set veth-app netns app-ns
```

Bring both ends up:

```bash
sudo ip link set veth-root up
sudo ip netns exec app-ns ip link set lo up
sudo ip netns exec app-ns ip link set veth-app up
```

Assign addresses — the host side becomes app-ns's gateway, the namespace side becomes app-ns's own address:

```bash
sudo ip addr add 10.30.0.1/24 dev veth-root
sudo ip netns exec app-ns ip addr add 10.30.0.2/24 dev veth-app
```

**Why it matters**: the moment you assign `10.30.0.2/24` to `veth-app`, the kernel automatically adds a directly-connected route for `10.30.0.0/24` inside the namespace — no `ip route add` needed for that part. You can confirm this now:

```bash
sudo ip netns exec app-ns ip route show
```

You will see exactly one line: `10.30.0.0/24 dev veth-app proto kernel scope link src 10.30.0.2`. One entry, one subnet. Nothing else is reachable yet — not because anything is broken, but because nothing else has been told to the namespace's routing table.

## Part 2: The Problem — Everything Outside 10.30.0.0/24

Try asking the kernel, from inside `app-ns`, how it would reach an address on a completely different network — say `203.0.113.5` (a documentation/test address, chosen because it is guaranteed not to collide with anything else in this lab):

```bash
sudo ip netns exec app-ns ip route get 203.0.113.5
```

Remember from the previous lab: `ip route get` performs a pure routing-table lookup — it does not send any packet, and the destination does not need to actually exist for the lookup to be meaningful. Right now, with only the directly-connected route in the table, this lookup fails: `RTNETLINK answers: Network is unreachable`. The kernel has no instruction for this destination and no fallback to try.

This is the exact failure a server has before it is given a gateway — it can talk to its own subnet and nothing more.

## Part 3: Adding the Default Route

A **default route** is written as the special destination `default` (equivalent to `0.0.0.0/0`, matching literally everything). It has the lowest possible priority — the kernel only falls back to it when no more specific route matches:

```bash
sudo ip netns exec app-ns ip route add default via 10.30.0.1
```

Verify it landed:

```bash
sudo ip netns exec app-ns ip route show
```

Now the table has two entries: the directly-connected `10.30.0.0/24`, and `default via 10.30.0.1 dev veth-app`. Every destination that isn't on the local subnet now has somewhere to go — `10.30.0.1`, the gateway on the other end of the veth pair.

## Part 4: Proving It With `ip route get`

Run the exact same lookup as before:

```bash
sudo ip netns exec app-ns ip route get 203.0.113.5
```

This time it succeeds, and the output shows the default route being used: `203.0.113.5 via 10.30.0.1 dev veth-app src 10.30.0.2`. Nothing about `10.30.0.0/24` changed — the kernel simply had nowhere else to look, so it fell through to the catch-all entry.

For contrast, check the gateway's own address:

```bash
sudo ip netns exec app-ns ip route get 10.30.0.1
```

This resolves via the **directly-connected** route, not the default one — no `via` in the output, because `10.30.0.1` is on the local subnet and needs no gateway to reach. The kernel always prefers the most specific match available; the default route is only ever a last resort.

**Why it matters**: this two-entry pattern — one directly-connected route per interface, plus a single default route for everything else — is the routing table of almost every ordinary Linux host and container you will ever manage. Understanding it here, in a namespace you fully control, is the same understanding you will apply to a production VM's `eth0` or a container's `eth0` inside Docker or Kubernetes.

## What's Next

The default route works — but what happens when it's wrong, or missing, or deleted by accident? Part 2 of this lab (CN-lab-03.2) picks up here and turns this into a troubleshooting exercise: inspecting the ARP cache the route produces traffic through, deliberately breaking the route, confirming the exact failure it causes, and restoring it — the diagnostic loop you'll run for real the first time a server "can reach its own subnet but nothing else."

## Conclusion

In this lab, you connected a namespace to the root namespace by giving it a default route:

- A fresh namespace's routing table starts with only the directly-connected route for whatever subnet you assigned an address on
- A default route (`ip route add default via <gateway>`) is the catch-all entry the kernel uses when nothing more specific matches
- `ip route get` proves, without sending any traffic, exactly which route an arbitrary destination will use — directly-connected addresses skip the gateway entirely, everything else falls through to `default`
- "Connecting to root" means giving a namespace a path through the host's own namespace, via the veth pair's host-side address acting as gateway
